title: Joining & Finishing Metals
description: Permanent joining (welding, brazing, soldering, riveting) and temporary; surface finishes and corrosion protection.
content_html:
Categories of Metal Joining

Metal components are joined either permanently (the joint is intended to be inseparable without destroying the parts) or temporarily (the joint can be disassembled and reassembled). Selecting the right joining method depends on the metals involved, the forces the joint must withstand, whether disassembly is needed for maintenance, and the required production speed.

Welding

Welding is the strongest permanent joining process for metals. It works by melting the parent (base) metal at the joint and, usually, adding a filler rod of similar composition. On cooling, the metals fuse into a single homogeneous joint. The three main arc-based welding processes are:

  • MIG welding (Metal Inert Gas) — a consumable wire electrode is automatically fed through the welding gun while a shielding gas (pure argon is inert for true MIG; an argon/CO&sub2; mix makes it MAG welding) protects the molten pool from atmospheric contamination. MIG is fast, easy to learn and suitable for steel and aluminium; widely used in automotive and general fabrication.
  • TIG welding (Tungsten Inert Gas) — a non-consumable tungsten electrode creates the arc; filler rod is added separately by hand. TIG produces a very clean, precise weld bead with excellent control over heat input. It is used for thin sheet, stainless steel, aluminium and titanium where weld quality is critical (aerospace, food equipment, artistic metalwork). TIG is slower and requires greater skill than MIG.
  • Arc welding (MMA — Manual Metal Arc) — a flux-coated electrode is used; the flux melts and forms a protective slag over the weld pool, eliminating the need for shielding gas. Simpler and cheaper equipment; suitable for outdoor use and for joining thick or rusty steel. The weld quality is generally lower than MIG or TIG and the slag must be chipped away after welding.
Key Fact

In welding, the base metal melts and fuses with a filler of the same composition — the joint becomes part of the parent material. In brazing and soldering, the base metal does NOT melt; only a lower-melting-point filler is melted and drawn into the joint by capillary action. Brazing uses filler melting above 450 °C; soldering uses filler melting below 450 °C.

Brazing and Soldering

Brazing uses a brass-based or silver-based filler alloy with a melting point above 450 °C (typically 700–900 °C). A flux is applied to prevent oxidation. The base metals are heated with an oxy-acetylene or propane torch until the filler melts and flows into the joint by capillary action. The joint is strong, neat and suitable for copper alloys and dissimilar metals. Brazed joints on copper pipe work and cycle frame lugs are common examples.

Soldering uses a tin-based filler alloy melting below 450 °C (soft solder melts at around 180–190 °C). It is used where low heat input is essential — electronic circuit boards (where high heat would destroy components), copper plumbing joints and jewellery. Flux is applied to clean the joint surfaces. Soldered joints are much weaker than brazed or welded joints and are not suitable where mechanical strength is the primary requirement. The critical difference from brazing is the lower temperature: in soldering the base metal remains entirely solid.

Riveting

Riveting is a permanent mechanical fastening method. A rivet is a short cylindrical pin with a preformed head. The plain (tail) end passes through pre-drilled holes in the parts being joined and is then deformed to form a second head, clamping the parts together. Riveting does not require heat and can join dissimilar metals. Pop rivets (blind rivets) can be set from one side only using a rivet gun; the mandrel is pulled through the rivet body, expanding the tail inside the joint, then snaps off. Pop rivets are widely used in aircraft skins, guttering and sheet metal enclosures. Traditional solid rivets (used in structural steelwork and older aircraft) require access to both sides and are stronger but slower to set.

Temporary Joining

Temporary joints can be disassembled without destroying either component. They are used wherever maintenance, adjustment or replacement of parts is required:

  • Nuts and bolts — the bolt passes through clearance holes in both parts; a nut is tightened onto the threaded end. Can be locked against loosening by a lock nut, spring washer or thread-locking adhesive. Suitable for heavy-duty structural joints (machinery, motor vehicle components).
  • Machine screws — similar to bolts but thread directly into a tapped (threaded) hole in one of the components, or into a threaded insert. Used in precision assemblies, electronics enclosures and consumer products where a clean appearance is needed (countersunk machine screws sit flush with the surface).
  • Self-tapping screws — cut their own thread as they are driven into a pre-drilled pilot hole; used for joining thin sheet metal without the need for a separate nut.

The choice between nuts and bolts, machine screws and self-tapping screws depends on the forces involved, the thickness of the material and whether a nut or tapped hole is feasible. Nuts and bolts provide the highest clamping force and can be torqued to a precise specification, making them suitable for safety-critical structural joints such as engine mountings. Machine screws suit precision enclosures where a flush appearance matters and the wall thickness allows tapping. Self-tapping screws offer the fastest assembly in thin sheet metal because no nut or separate tapping operation is needed.

The three thermal joining processes are frequently confused. The key distinguishing variable is whether the parent metal melts. In welding (MIG, TIG, arc) the parent metal reaches its melting point and the filler is the same or similar alloy; the cooled joint is essentially continuous with the parent material. In brazing the parent does not melt (it is kept below its melting point); the filler (brass or silver alloy, above 450 °C) flows into the gap by capillary action and bonds metallurgically. In soldering the parent again does not melt; the filler (tin-based, below 450 °C) flows in by capillary action and bonds by adhesion and limited diffusion. Joint strength decreases in the sequence welding > brazing > soldering.

Temperature comparison: arc welding steel reaches approximately 3,500 °C at the arc; brazing with a propane torch might heat the joint to 750 °C; soldering a circuit board operates at around 250 °C. These temperature differences explain why soldering is safe for delicate electronic components but welding would destroy them instantly.

Surface Finishes and Corrosion Protection

Most ferrous metals corrode when exposed to moisture and oxygen; many non-ferrous metals also deteriorate in certain environments. Surface finishes serve two main purposes: protecting the metal from corrosion and improving its appearance. Common surface treatments include:

  • Painting — the simplest and most versatile finish. A primer is applied first to improve adhesion and provide an initial corrosion barrier; topcoat paint provides colour and further protection. Breaks in the paint film expose the metal to corrosion, so surface preparation (cleaning, degreasing, sanding or shot-blasting) is critical for paint adhesion.
  • Powder coating — dry polymer powder is electrostatically applied to the metal surface and then cured in an oven at 180–200 °C, fusing into a tough, uniform film. Provides better impact resistance, corrosion resistance and consistency of finish than liquid paint. Used on bicycle frames, garden furniture and electrical enclosures.
  • Electroplating — a thin layer of a corrosion-resistant or decorative metal (chrome, nickel, zinc, gold) is deposited onto the base metal using an electrolytic process. Chromium plating on taps and car trim provides a bright, hard, corrosion-resistant surface; zinc electroplating (electro-galvanising) provides sacrificial protection to steel.
  • Anodising — an electrochemical process specific to aluminium. The aluminium is made the anode in an electrolytic bath; this thickens the natural oxide layer on the surface, greatly improving corrosion and abrasion resistance. The porous anodised layer can be dyed in a wide range of colours before sealing. Used on bicycle components, laptop cases and sporting equipment.
  • Galvanising — steel is dipped in molten zinc (hot-dip galvanising), coating it with a tough zinc layer. The zinc provides both a physical barrier and sacrificial protection: zinc is more reactive than iron, so it corrodes preferentially if the coating is damaged, protecting the underlying steel. Used on fence posts, crash barriers, steel road signs and structural steelwork.
  • Dip coating (plastic dip coating) — the metal is preheated and dipped into a tank of powdered or liquid thermoplastic (often PVC or polyethylene). The plastic melts onto the surface and solidifies as a thick, flexible, grip-able coating. Used on tool handles, garden tools, dishwasher baskets and wire shelving. Provides excellent grip, insulation and corrosion protection.
  • Polishing — progressive abrasion using finer and finer abrasives, finishing with a buffing compound, produces a mirror-like surface on metals such as stainless steel, aluminium and copper. Used for decorative products (trophies, jewellery, cookware). Polishing is a surface preparation, not a corrosion barrier — a polished surface must still be lacquered or otherwise protected if corrosion resistance is required.
Key Fact

Galvanising applies to steel and uses a zinc coating that provides sacrificial protection (the zinc corrodes first). Anodising applies only to aluminium and is an electrochemical process that thickens the existing oxide layer; it does not involve a separate metal coating. Confusing the two is a frequent exam error.
exam_tip_html: For any question comparing welding, brazing and soldering, the examiner is looking for you to identify: (1) whether the base metal melts, (2) the filler material and its melting point range, and (3) the resulting joint strength or application. A Mastering-level answer for a 6-mark question would also include a specific product example for each process and comment on the skill or equipment required. Do not just say a joint is “stronger” — explain why (e.g. “welding fuses the base metal, making the joint continuous with the parent material, whereas soldering only adheres a low-melting-point filler to the surface”).
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Welding melts the base metal and produces the strongest joint; brazing uses filler above 450 degrees Celsius without melting the base metal; soldering uses filler below 450 degrees Celsius and is suitable only where low heat is essential and high strength is not required.
  • Riveting (especially pop rivets) and threaded fasteners (nuts, bolts, machine screws) provide permanent and temporary mechanical joints respectively, without heat.
  • Surface finishes protect metals from corrosion and improve appearance; galvanising gives steel sacrificial zinc protection, anodising electrochemically thickens aluminium's oxide layer, and powder coating provides a tough and uniform polymer film.

glossary_terms.definition: A joining process in which the base metals themselves are melted and fused together, usually with a filler of the same composition; produces a joint as strong as or stronger than the parent material.

A joining process in which a brass-based filler alloy with a melting point above 450 degrees Celsius is melted and drawn into the gap between two base metals by capillary action; the base metals themselves do not melt.
A joining process using a tin-based filler with a melting point below 450 degrees Celsius; used for electronic components or copper pipework where low heat input is required.
Coating steel with a layer of molten zinc to provide a physical barrier and sacrificial corrosion protection; zinc corrodes preferentially if the coating is damaged.

practice_questions.text:

practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two of: painting / powder coating / galvanising / electroplating (zinc) / dip coating / primer application. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how galvanising protects steel from corrosion.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per clear, distinct point up to 3:
• The steel is dipped into a bath of molten zinc, which coats the surface with a layer of zinc.
• The zinc provides a physical barrier preventing moisture and oxygen reaching the steel surface.
• If the coating is scratched, the zinc acts as a sacrificial anode and corrodes preferentially, continuing to protect the exposed steel beneath because zinc is more reactive than iron. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the differences between welding, brazing and soldering as methods of permanently joining metals.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• In welding, the base metals are heated to their melting point and fuse together with a filler of the same composition; the joint becomes part of the parent material and is as strong as or stronger than the base metal.
• In brazing, the base metal does not melt; a brass or silver-based filler alloy with a melting point above 450°C is melted by a torch and flows into the joint by capillary action.
• In soldering, the base metal again does not melt; a tin-based filler with a melting point below 450°C is used; the joint is weaker than a brazed or welded joint.
• Soldering is therefore used where heat input must be minimised (e.g. electronic circuit boards) and structural strength is not the priority.
[4 marks: 1 mark per clear developed point]

practice_questions.text: Explain why powder coating is preferred over liquid paint for the finish on a steel bicycle frame intended for year-round outdoor use.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Powder coating is applied as a dry electrostatic powder and cured at 180-200°C, producing a chemically cross-linked polymer film that bonds strongly to the metal surface.
• The resulting coating is significantly harder and more impact-resistant than conventional liquid paint, which is important for a bicycle frame exposed to stone chips and knocks.
• Powder coating provides a more uniform film thickness with no runs or drips, improving the visual quality and consistency of the finish.
• It is more resistant to chipping and scratching, meaning the steel is less likely to be exposed to moisture and therefore less likely to corrode at damage points.
• Powder coating produces very low VOC (volatile organic compound) emissions compared to solvent-based paints, making it more environmentally responsible.
• For liquid paint to perform comparably, multiple priming and topcoat layers would be needed, increasing production time and cost; powder coating achieves a superior result in a single cure step.
[6 marks — Mastering: At least three specific advantages of powder coating linked to the bicycle-frame context with reference to corrosion, mechanical properties and process efficiency. Secure: Two advantages with some development. Developing: One advantage; limited development or context. Emerging: Vague preference stated without explanation.]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using MIG welding compared to riveting for permanently joining mild steel panels in the manufacture of a car body.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages of MIG welding:
• MIG welding fuses the base metal together, producing a continuous joint that is as strong as the parent material; this is important for crash safety and structural integrity.
• Automated MIG welding robots operate at very high speed on a production line, reducing cycle time and labour cost per vehicle.
• Welded joints create a smooth, flush surface that is ideal for applying primer and paint without the raised heads associated with rivets.
• No holes need to be drilled through the panels prior to joining, reducing the risk of stress concentrations at hole edges.
Disadvantages of MIG welding:
• The heat introduced during welding can cause distortion and warping of thin sheet panels, requiring subsequent straightening operations.
• Welded joints are permanent; if a panel needs replacement after a minor collision, the weld must be cut away, increasing repair cost and time.
• MIG welding of coated or galvanised steel may produce toxic fumes from the zinc coating, requiring extraction and PPE.
• Riveting by comparison is fast to set up for low volume, requires no heat, can join dissimilar metals and is easily disassembled; however, rivet heads are visible and the joint is weaker in tension than an equivalent weld.
[8 marks — Mastering: Sustained, balanced discussion of at least two developed advantages and two disadvantages of MIG welding relative to riveting, linked to car body manufacturing context (strength, speed, surface finish, repairability). Secure: Two advantages and two disadvantages with some development. Developing: Points listed with limited development; little balance. Emerging: One-sided or superficial.]

knowledge_checks.q: Which joining process does NOT melt the base metal and uses a filler with a melting point below 450°C?
Which surface treatment is specific to aluminium and thickens its natural oxide layer electrochemically?
In welding, the base metal _____ and fuses with a filler of the same composition.
Galvanising protects steel by coating it with _____, which corrodes sacrificially if the coating is damaged.

right: Set from one side only using a rivet gun; mandrel snaps off
Non-consumable tungsten electrode; precise, clean weld bead

flashcard_questions.q: In welding, does the base metal melt?
flashcard_questions.a: Yes; the base metal melts and fuses with a filler of the same composition.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the key difference between brazing and soldering?
flashcard_questions.a: Brazing filler melts above 450 degrees Celsius; soldering filler melts below 450 degrees Celsius.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is soldering used for electronic circuit boards rather than brazing?
flashcard_questions.a: Soldering operates at low temperature (around 250 degrees Celsius), preventing heat damage to components.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a pop rivet and from how many sides can it be set?
flashcard_questions.a: A blind rivet set from one side only using a rivet gun; the mandrel expands the tail and snaps off.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between MIG and TIG welding?
flashcard_questions.a: MIG uses a consumable wire electrode fed automatically; TIG uses a non-consumable tungsten electrode with filler added by hand.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is TIG welding preferred for thin stainless steel?
flashcard_questions.a: TIG gives precise heat control, a clean weld bead and minimal distortion on thin or delicate material.

flashcard_questions.q: How does galvanising provide sacrificial protection?
flashcard_questions.a: Zinc is more reactive than iron; if the coating is scratched, zinc corrodes preferentially, protecting the steel.

flashcard_questions.q: Which metal does anodising apply to, and what does it do?
flashcard_questions.a: Aluminium; anodising electrochemically thickens the natural oxide layer, improving corrosion and abrasion resistance.

flashcard_questions.q: What advantage does powder coating have over liquid paint for a bicycle frame?
flashcard_questions.a: It produces a harder, more impact-resistant film with better corrosion protection and no runs or drips.

flashcard_questions.q: What does dip coating involve and what property does it add?
flashcard_questions.a: Preheated metal is dipped in thermoplastic powder or liquid; adds grip, insulation and corrosion protection.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one temporary and one permanent mechanical fastening method for metals.
flashcard_questions.a: Temporary: nut and bolt. Permanent: riveting.

flashcard_questions.q: In what order do welding, brazing and soldering rank by joint strength?
flashcard_questions.a: Welding is strongest, then brazing, then soldering.
